58:11.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا قِيلَ لَكُمۡ تَفَسَّحُواْ فِي ٱلۡمَجَٰلِسِ فَٱفۡسَحُواْ يَفۡسَحِ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡۖ وَإِذَا قِيلَ ٱنشُزُواْ فَٱنشُزُواْ يَرۡفَعِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ مِنكُمۡ وَٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلۡعِلۡمَ دَرَجَٰتࣲۚ وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣱ‏
58:11.en: O ye who believe! when it is said unto you, Make room! in assemblies, then make room; Allah will make way for you (hereafter). And when it is said, Come up higher! go up higher; Allah will exalt those who believe among you, and those who have knowledge, to high ranks. Allah is Informed of what ye do

58:12.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا نَٰجَيۡتُمُ ٱلرَّسُولَ فَقَدِّمُواْ بَيۡنَ يَدَيۡ نَجۡوَىٰكُمۡ صَدَقَةࣰۚ ذَٰلِكَ خَيۡرࣱ لَّكُمۡ وَأَطۡهَرُۚ فَإِن لَّمۡ تَجِدُواْ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمٌ
58:12.en: O ye who believe! When ye hold conference with the messenger, offer an alms before your conference. That is better and purer for you. But if ye cannot find (the wherewithal) then lo! Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

58:13.ar: ءَأَشۡفَقۡتُمۡ أَن تُقَدِّمُواْ بَيۡنَ يَدَيۡ نَجۡوَىٰكُمۡ صَدَقَٰتࣲۚ فَإِذۡ لَمۡ تَفۡعَلُواْ وَتَابَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ فَأَقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُواْ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَأَطِيعُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥۚ وَٱللَّهُ خَبِيرُۢ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ
58:13.en: Fear ye to offer alms before your conference? Then, when ye do it not and Allah hath forgiven you, establish worship and pay the poor-due and obey Allah and His messenger. And Allah is Aware of what ye do

58:1.ar: قَدۡ سَمِعَ ٱللَّهُ قَوۡلَ ٱلَّتِي تُجَٰدِلُكَ فِي زَوۡجِهَا وَتَشۡتَكِيٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَٱللَّهُ يَسۡمَعُ تَحَاوُرَكُمَآۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَمِيعُۢ بَصِيرٌ
58:1.en: Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee (Muhammad) concerning her husband, and complaineth unto Allah. And Allah heareth your colloquy. Lo! Allah is Hearer, Knower

58:2.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يُظَٰهِرُونَ مِنكُم مِّن نِّسَآئِهِم مَّا هُنَّ أُمَّهَٰتِهِمۡۖ إِنۡ أُمَّهَٰتُهُمۡ إِلَّا ٱلَّٰٓـِٔي وَلَدۡنَهُمۡۚ وَإِنَّهُمۡ لَيَقُولُونَ مُنكَرࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلۡقَوۡلِ وَزُورࣰ اۚ وَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورࣱ‏
58:2.en: Such of you as put away your wives (by saying they are as their mothers) - They are not their mothers; none are their mothers except those who gave them birth - they indeed utter an ill word and a lie. And lo! Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

58:3.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ يُظَٰهِرُونَ مِن نِّسَآئِهِمۡ ثُمَّ يَعُودُونَ لِمَا قَالُواْ فَتَحۡرِيرُ رَقَبَةࣲ مِّن قَبۡلِ أَن يَتَمَآسَّاۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ تُوعَظُونَ بِهِۦۚ وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣱ‏
58:3.en: Those who put away their wives (by saying they are as their mothers) and afterward would go back on that which they have said, (the penalty) in that case (is) the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. Unto this ye are exhorted; and Allah is Informed of what ye do

58:4.ar: فَمَن لَّمۡ يَجِدۡ فَصِيَامُ شَهۡرَيۡنِ مُتَتَابِعَيۡنِ مِن قَبۡلِ أَن يَتَمَآسَّاۖ فَمَن لَّمۡ يَسۡتَطِعۡ فَإِطۡعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسۡكِينࣰ اۚ ذَٰلِكَ لِتُؤۡمِنُواْ بِٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦۚ وَتِلۡكَ حُدُودُ ٱللَّهِۗ وَلِلۡكَٰفِرِينَ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ
58:4.en: And he who findeth not (the wherewithal), let him fast for two successive months before they touch one another; and for him who is unable to do so (the penance is) the feeding of sixty needy ones. This, that ye may put trust in Allah and His messenger. Such are the limits (imposed by Allah); and for disbelievers is a painful doom

58:7.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَعۡلَمُ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ مَا يَكُونُ مِن نَّجۡوَىٰ ثَلَٰثَةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ رَابِعُهُمۡ وَلَا خَمۡسَةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ سَادِسُهُمۡ وَلَآ أَدۡنَىٰ مِن ذَٰلِكَ وَلَآ أَكۡثَرَ إِلَّا هُوَ مَعَهُمۡ أَيۡنَ مَا كَانُواْۖ ثُمَّ يُنَبِّئُهُم بِمَا عَمِلُواْ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِكُلِّ شَيۡءٍ عَلِيمٌ
58:7.en: Hast thou not seen that Allah knoweth all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth? There is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth, nor of five but He is their sixth, nor of less than that or more but He is with them wheresoever they may be; and afterward, on the Day of Resurrection, He will inform them of what they did. Lo! Allah is Knower of all things

58:8.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ إِلَى ٱلَّذِينَ نُهُواْ عَنِ ٱلنَّجۡوَىٰ ثُمَّ يَعُودُونَ لِمَا نُهُواْ عَنۡهُ وَيَتَنَٰجَوۡنَ بِٱلۡإِثۡمِ وَٱلۡعُدۡوَٰنِ وَمَعۡصِيَتِ ٱلرَّسُولِۖ وَإِذَا جَآءُوكَ حَيَّوۡكَ بِمَا لَمۡ يُحَيِّكَ بِهِ ٱللَّهُ وَيَقُولُونَ فِيٓ أَنفُسِهِمۡ لَوۡلَا يُعَذِّبُنَا ٱللَّهُ بِمَا نَقُولُۚ حَسۡبُهُمۡ جَهَنَّمُ يَصۡلَوۡنَهَاۖ فَبِئۡسَ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ
58:8.en: Hast thou not observed those who were forbidden conspiracy and afterward returned to that which they had been forbidden, and (now) conspire together for crime and wrongdoing and disobedience toward the messenger? And when they come unto thee they greet thee with a greeting wherewith Allah greeteth thee not, and say within themselves: Why should Allah punish us for what we say? Hell will suffice them; they will feel the heat thereof - a hapless journey's end

58:9.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا تَنَٰجَيۡتُمۡ فَلَا تَتَنَٰجَوۡاْ بِٱلۡإِثۡمِ وَٱلۡعُدۡوَٰنِ وَمَعۡصِيَتِ ٱلرَّسُولِ وَتَنَٰجَوۡاْ بِٱلۡبِرِّ وَٱلتَّقۡوَىٰۖ وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ ٱلَّذِيٓ إِلَيۡهِ تُحۡشَرُونَ
58:9.en: O ye who believe! When ye conspire together, conspire not together for crime and wrongdoing and disobedience toward the messenger, but conspire together for righteousness and piety, and keep your duty toward Allah, unto whom ye will be gathered

58:10.ar: إِنَّمَا ٱلنَّجۡوَىٰ مِنَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ لِيَحۡزُنَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَلَيۡسَ بِضَآرِّهِمۡ شَيۡـًٔا إِلَّا بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَعَلَى ٱللَّهِ فَلۡيَتَوَكَّلِ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ
58:10.en: Lo! Conspiracy is only of the devil, that he may vex those who believe; but he can harm them not at all unless by Allah's leave. In Allah let believers put their trust

qlHfIJf1h6Y.speaker: adnan
qlHfIJf1h6Y.speaker_note: his own Sunday tafseer series; speaks of his own khutbahs, skills and parents
qlHfIJf1h6Y.title: Sunday Tafseer: Surat Al-Mujadilah, Part 3 (Verses 11-13)
qlHfIJf1h6Y.one_line: Making room for everyone, moving when asked, raising the qualified, and giving back before taking the leader's private time.
qlHfIJf1h6Y.summary: He reviews the surah's lessons so far: oppression is never tolerated, and najwa, breakaway lobbying after collective decisions, is what cripples Muslim institutions in the West. He warns against chronic complainers, explains that the minbar's job is to provoke thought rather than please, and insists a minority community cannot afford division: every mosque is part of one bigger picture, and Andalus fell when each kingdom thought it could stand alone. Verse eleven literally tells people to make room in gatherings and to rise when asked, but he reads it organizationally: everyone must have a place and a voice, and when asked to move to a different role you accept it, because Allah raises those with faith and knowledge. Communities fail when untrained people lead or give fatwas, when there is no mentoring, and since families and communities gave up the elder system. The experienced person's wrong decision beats the novice's right one. Verses twelve and thirteen required charity before a private session with the Prophet; he draws three lessons: whoever takes from the community must give back, leaders should not seek money, and leaders' time must be protected. Prayer and zakat stand for personal and people-serving worship.

outline.heading: Opening
The last four juz as the condensed Quran
outline.gist: If memorizing is hard, learn Qaf to An-Nas well; it holds every type of surah, structure and theme.

outline.heading: The cluster organizes the Muslim community
outline.gist: The late Madinan surahs of juz 28 cover how Muslims organize among themselves and with others.

outline.heading: Review, theme one: oppression is never tolerated
outline.gist: Zihar was a sneaky way to trap wives, and Allah attached a heavy penalty to it.

outline.heading: Review, theme two: najwa as breakaway consultation
outline.gist: Explaining it as excluding a third person is fine for children; it is about side groups that build resentment after decisions.

outline.heading: Why we are not getting anywhere in the West
outline.gist: Boards of twelve with fake smiles who complain afterwards and own nothing.

outline.heading: Not being punished does not make it right
outline.gist: Allah gives time but does not forget; any private talk should push the work forward.

outline.heading: Complainers drain a minority community
outline.gist: Work with whatever positivity exists; pointing out problems is the minbar's job, not the bystander's.

outline.heading: The Prophet on the minbar and the purpose of a khutbah
outline.gist: The gentle Prophet's face reddened and his voice rose as if warning of an army; a khutbah should leave you struggling with something.

outline.heading: Easy popularity versus knowledge that points out deficits
outline.gist: Saying what people want is safe and changes nothing; no one wants to change their own behaviour.

outline.heading: He starts with himself; the hard questions of Hadid
outline.gist: He speaks of faults he sees in himself first; the earlier surahs asked about purpose, guidance, certainty and balance.

outline.heading: A minority cannot afford division
outline.gist: These verses came to a majority; as a minority we must work with and promote every mosque even when we disagree.

outline.heading: Getting over the ego
outline.gist: An imam who says his community needs no one else has slipped.

outline.heading: Andalus: kingdoms that stood alone and fell
outline.gist: A civilization rich in books and the language of learning fell kingdom by kingdom; do not entertain going it alone.

outline.heading: Interlude
Make room in gatherings and rise when asked: the plain meaning
outline.gist: Open space for others, especially elders, and Allah will open space for you.

outline.heading: The people of Badr given seats in front
outline.gist: The reported occasion, whose authenticity is questioned.

outline.heading: Figurative space: room to speak and belong
outline.gist: No Muslim should have to fight for a place or a voice in the community.

outline.heading: Rising: accepting a different role
outline.gist: When told this is not your spot, move; a community needs every type of person, not only those at the microphone.

outline.heading: Allah raises those of faith and knowledge
outline.gist: People without the needed knowledge in key positions is the core problem; everyone thinks they are knowledgeable.

outline.heading: Respect expertise: stop giving fatwas from YouTube
outline.gist: A year of listening to a sheikh is not an education; he would not argue medicine from a pathology book or tell a plumber what to do.

outline.heading: Companions served wherever they were placed
outline.gist: An early companion told he should not lead even two people accepted it and never became disgruntled.

outline.heading: It is about skill, not worth: and we have no mentoring
outline.gist: Being told a role is not for you is not a judgment of your value; without coaching everyone tries to do everything.

outline.heading: What we lost when we gave up elders
outline.gist: Families and communities need experienced, wise people to resolve disputes; a Syrian proverb says if you have no elder, find one.

outline.heading: Find your elder: he never regretted listening to his parents
outline.gist: No one has it figured out; the 39-year-old you will understand what the 19-year-old could not see.

outline.heading: The experienced person's wrong decision beats the novice's right one
outline.gist: A minority community cannot be a training ground for someone's leadership skills; seek out and beg qualified people to lead.

outline.heading: Without the first half of the verse the second fails
outline.gist: If people are not welcomed and heard, they will not accept being moved by merit.

outline.heading: Khabir: Allah knows the inner motive
outline.gist: Each name of knowledge has its target; Khabir points to what is in the self, such as why you resist someone more qualified.

outline.heading: Summary: give space, then put people in the right places
outline.gist: Communities need few scholars but many people with financial, managerial, social and therapeutic skills.

outline.heading: Recitation note: when the noon disappears into lam
outline.gist: Complete merging without nasal sound, and knowing where the noon is written in the mushaf.

outline.heading: Interlude
A different najwa: private counsel with the Prophet
outline.gist: The same word now means seeking a private session with the leader, which is not the harmful kind.

outline.heading: Everyone wanted a piece of his time
outline.gist: His endless compassion hid his fatigue, and people brought him every family problem and dream.

outline.heading: Charity before the private session
outline.gist: Rather than telling people to stop coming, Allah asked them to give first, which makes them think twice.

outline.heading: Why it is purer for you
outline.gist: Burdening the Prophet risks Allah's displeasure; the charity purifies that harm.

outline.heading: Relief for those who cannot pay
outline.gist: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful; those who could not give were still welcome, and Allah turned to them.

outline.heading: Prayer and zakat as the two kinds of worship
outline.gist: Salah stands for worship between you and Allah, zakat for worship that benefits others; together they cover all worship.

outline.heading: Whoever takes from the community must give back
outline.gist: The Prophet took nothing for himself; if you expect services from the mosque, what are you contributing?

outline.heading: Give what you can; leaders should not seek money
outline.gist: Those who had private time with him had something to envy; give wealth or at least a high standard of conduct.

outline.heading: Respect leaders' time
outline.gist: Do not overburden those whose time belongs to the group.

outline.heading: Khabir moved forward: Allah's care for the leader's wellbeing
outline.gist: Changed word order emphasizes that Allah knows your real intention and cares that leaders can do their job.

24:32.ar: وَأَنكِحُواْ ٱلۡأَيَٰمَىٰ مِنكُمۡ وَٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ مِنۡ عِبَادِكُمۡ وَإِمَآئِكُمۡۚ إِن يَكُونُواْ فُقَرَآءَ يُغۡنِهِمُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضۡلِهِۦۗ وَٱللَّهُ وَٰسِعٌ عَلِيمࣱ‏
24:32.en: And marry such of you as are solitary and the pious of your slaves and maid-servants. If they be poor, Allah will enrich them of His bounty. Allah is of ample means, Aware

30:21.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦٓ أَنۡ خَلَقَ لَكُم مِّنۡ أَنفُسِكُمۡ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ ا لِّتَسۡكُنُوٓاْ إِلَيۡهَا وَجَعَلَ بَيۡنَكُم مَّوَدَّةࣰ وَرَحۡمَةًۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّقَوۡمࣲ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ
30:21.en: And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy. Lo! herein indeed are portents for folk who reflect

2Z--EEoHzfU.speaker_note: single voice; opens his own marriage sub-series, mentions being Syrian and ten years of seeing marriage problems
2Z--EEoHzfU.title: Tackling Contemporary Issues: Marriage (Part 1)
2Z--EEoHzfU.one_line: Four points for starting marriages well: secure parental acceptance early, prepare, apply compatibility without racism, and treat mahr as a gift, not a price.
2Z--EEoHzfU.summary: He opens with the command to marry off the single and the verse on spouses as a sign of love and mercy, calling marriage a universal human institution and a prophetic Sunnah. He reviews the hadith urging young people to marry or else practise restraint, choosing a spouse for faith over beauty, lineage or wealth, and accepting a suitor whose character and religion you are pleased with. Drawing on patterns he has seen for ten years, he gives four points. First, before getting attached, make sure both sets of parents are broadly open to the match, or someone will be hurt. Second, marriage needs psychological, religious, financial and social preparation, ideally through professional workshops. Third, kafa'ah, compatibility, is a real parental duty, but refusing someone over race, nationality or city is racism, and a refusal must be explained. Fourth, mahr reflects the man's ability, not the woman's worth; treating it as a price or insurance is a jahiliyyah mindset that breeds resentment while haram is easy for the young. Whoever wants extras should pay, and Ali's mahr was a shield. He condemns a father's double standard between his son's and daughter's mahr, then closes by urging everyone to bring back to the masjid the many local Muslims who never attend.

outline.heading: Opening
Marriage as Allah's Sunnah
outline.gist: An-Nur's command to marry off the single and Ar-Rum's verse on spouses as a sign of love and mercy; marriage taught since Adam and Eve; third topic in the contemporary issues series, no substitute for counselling.

outline.heading: A universal institution, and the call to the young
outline.gist: Every culture and era has had marriage; it is the Sunnah of the prophets; the Prophet tells young people who are able to marry to do so.

outline.heading: Restraint, and choosing for faith
outline.gist: Those who cannot marry must hold back from whatever leads to haram, wider than ritual fasting; of the four reasons a woman is married, choose faith.

outline.heading: Accept a suitor of faith and character
outline.gist: The hadith on accepting a suitor whose religion and character please you, and the scholar who told a father to choose the God-fearing man.

outline.heading: Ten recurring patterns, and why they matter
outline.gist: He is no marriage counsellor; his ten points come from problems repeated over ten years, not individuals; neglecting marriage leaves the community a grim future.

outline.heading: The five Ps when marriage is not the aim
outline.gist: Recap of the rule for dealing with the other gender: professional, pious, protective, part ways, pleasant; marriage is the only acceptable aim otherwise.

outline.heading: Point one: secure parental acceptance first
outline.gist: The rookie move is getting attached and then telling parents; when a family refuses, someone is badly hurt, so check both families are broadly open before pursuing someone.

outline.heading: Point two: prepare on every level
outline.gist: Psychological, religious, financial, social and academic preparation; two universes collide in a marriage and the unprepared suffer avoidable pain.

outline.heading: Expectations decide the first year
outline.gist: A question or two to an engaged couple tells him how their first year will go; professionals must prepare the psychological side, his khutbahs will cover the religious rights and duties.

outline.heading: Point three: kafa'ah is the parents' duty
outline.gist: Kafa'ah means compatibility or equivalency; both families must assess it, knowing their own child, and any refusal must be explained honestly.

outline.heading: Refusing over race or origin is racism
outline.gist: Rejecting an excellent suitor because of skin colour, nationality or city is racism that sickens him; parents must not misuse their role.

outline.heading: What kafa'ah actually protects
outline.gist: Its purpose is that a wife is cared for as she was at home so neither is miserable, not country, race or money.

outline.heading: Point four: mahr is a gift, not a price
outline.gist: Mahr is measured by the man's ability as a sign of commitment; a fixed price on a daughter is the practice of jahiliyyah, and a high mahr is no insurance against a bad husband.

outline.heading: Resentment and the man's only obligations
outline.gist: High demands plant resentment in the groom; besides mahr his only financial duty is maintenance, yet cultures add four to seven extra demands.

outline.heading: Haram is easy, so marriage must be easy
outline.gist: A 25-year-old does not have that money; haram reaches young people effortlessly, so marriage must be at least as easy.

outline.heading: Whoever wants extras pays for them
outline.gist: Large sums for weddings could clear debt or buy a home; the party who wants the extra pays, which is the historical Islamic norm.

outline.heading: Ali's shield
outline.gist: Only a jahili mindset calls a small mahr cheap; Ali's mahr for Fatimah was his shield, yet no marriage had more barakah or preserved more.

outline.heading: Easing marriage is a duty on all
outline.gist: He sets no numbers; the aim is facilitation so people avoid haram and build families, and high numbers, poor preparation and racist barriers all work against it.

outline.heading: A father's double standard
outline.gist: The same father resented his son's costly mahr and three years later demanded double for his daughter.

outline.heading: Easing entry alone is not enough
outline.gist: If the match is wrong, say so plainly rather than playing with numbers; easing the start of marriage will not fix the problems that threaten its longevity.

outline.heading: Bring back Muslims who never come
outline.gist: Of about 30,000 local Muslims only around 4,000 attend Jumuah; the masjid's job is to welcome them and each person's job is to bring someone, especially the young.

outline.heading: Outro

HQKx71ZWTLU.title: Arabic Tafsir of Surat Sad: Obedience as Returning to the Truth, Verses 1-7
HQKx71ZWTLU.one_line: Surat Sad's axis is obeying Allah by returning to the truth; legitimate disagreement, the overuse of 'bid'ah', tajweed, and Quraysh's pride and defiance.
HQKx71ZWTLU.summary: Opening Surat Sad, the sheikh places it in the sequence from al-Ahzab to az-Zumar on obedience to Allah, and names its theme: obeying Allah by returning to the truth once you see you were wrong. The ego resists admitting error, especially to someone it dislikes; Umar was 'one who stops at the Book of Allah', who conceded on the minbar to a woman about dowries. He warns against misusing this: when someone hears your argument and keeps his view, he may simply have reached a different conclusion, and most fiqh questions allow legitimate difference among the schools. Non-specialists should follow a scholar rather than form views from videos, should not 'strike people with hadith', and should stop calling minor practices such as saying 'Jumuah Mubarak' or wiping the face after dua bid'ah. Returning to the truth requires actually seeking it, standing for justice even against oneself and those one dislikes. After notes on the surah's late Meccan context, the disjointed letters and detailed tajweed of qalqalah and makhraj, he explains 'the Quran of remembrance': it reminds the innate faith people already have. The disbelievers' problem was not ignorance but pride and defiance; at death there is no time to return. Quraysh resorted to character attacks, calling the Prophet a lying sorcerer, and Abu Jahl and Musaylimah's followers admitted tribal pride outweighed truth.

outline.heading: Opening
Surat Sad is a delight to explain
outline.gist: Its purpose is clear and its expression firm.

outline.heading: The axis from al-Ahzab to az-Zumar: obedience in different conditions
outline.gist: Al-Ahzab on obedience under hardship, Saba on communities obeying with knowledge, Ya-Sin on da'wah, as-Saffat on the unseen.

outline.heading: Surat Sad: obedience by returning to the truth
outline.gist: The ego finds nothing harder than admitting it was wrong, especially when the other side is someone it dislikes; every story in the surah turns on this.

outline.heading: Umar conceded to a woman on the minbar
outline.gist: He was known as one who stops at the Book of Allah; when a woman objected to his ruling on dowries he said 'the woman is right and Umar is wrong', though his view was sound.

outline.heading: The road back to truth is rugged
outline.gist: The soul throws up a million obstacles; between spouses there is almost no hope.

outline.heading: Bring your proof, but do not misuse the idea
outline.gist: A Muslim follows evidence, but someone who keeps his view after hearing you may have already weighed your point.

outline.heading: Disagreement among the schools is legitimate
outline.gist: You may reach your own view in disputed fiqh, but cannot deny others theirs; condemning other madhhabs was a fashion of the 1980s.

outline.heading: Follow a scholar; do not build views from videos
outline.gist: Only foundational beliefs are beyond dispute; non-specialists should follow a scholar and not advise on disputed matters.

outline.heading: Do not strike people with hadith
outline.gist: Scholars weighed the Quran, hadith, Madinan practice, Companions, language and objectives and reached different conclusions; even some belief questions admit difference.

outline.heading: The word 'bid'ah' is not to be thrown around
outline.gist: Questions about saying 'Jumuah Mubarak' and wiping the face after dua show how the heavy word has been cheapened.

outline.heading: You cannot return to truth unless you seek it
outline.gist: The Prophet stood alone against Mecca because no proof had shown him wrong; objectivity means truth is the highest value.

outline.heading: Standing for justice even against yourself
outline.gist: Do not let hatred of a people make you unjust; Islam is commitment to the truth in every state.

outline.heading: Badr: the truth over the caravan
outline.gist: The Companions wanted the unarmed caravan, but Allah willed to establish the truth; claim your right before choosing to give it away.

outline.heading: Surat Sad is late Meccan, without an occasion of revelation
outline.gist: Late Meccan surahs prepared the Prophet's heart for migration and leadership.

outline.heading: The disjointed letters as a challenge and a code
outline.gist: The Quran is made of the letters they know; Said Hawwa's study of letters linking surahs, such as the Ha-Mim group.

outline.heading: Tajweed: six-count madd in the disjointed letters
outline.gist: The letters of 'naqas 'asalkum' are elongated six counts; how to join Ya-Sin and Nun with what follows in Hafs.

outline.heading: Tajweed: major and minor qalqalah
outline.gist: Most verse endings in Sad end in qalqalah; qalqalah is major when the speech stops, not when the word ends, and is a vibration, not a vowel.

outline.heading: A blind teacher heard a reader move his head
outline.gist: His teacher corrected head movement by ear; each letter has a fixed point of articulation that must not be helped by the body.

outline.heading: Honour the letters and the limits of the Quran
outline.gist: Precise recitation is reverence; the Quran is preserved in hearts, and the answer to neglecting its limits is not to neglect its letters.

outline.heading: Recitation of the opening verses
'The Quran of remembrance': it reminds you of what you know
outline.gist: Returning to truth is remembering; Allah placed faith in human nature at the covenant.

outline.heading: Their problem was pride and defiance, not forgetting
outline.gist: 'Bal' corrects: they remembered, but pride held them; shiqaq is seeing the truth and refusing it.

outline.heading: 'No longer the time of escape'
outline.gist: At destruction they called out, but the time to return had passed; return before it is said to you.

outline.heading: Amazed that a warner came from among them
outline.gist: He was described first as a warner, because failing to warn of punishment is worse than failing to promise reward.

outline.heading: 'A lying sorcerer': attacking the person when the argument fails
outline.gist: Unable to answer the Quran, they attacked his character, the trick of politicians.

outline.heading: 'Has he made the gods one God?'
outline.gist: Every atom to galaxy follows one law; multiple gods are logically impossible.

outline.heading: 'Be patient with your gods': rhetoric that leads to ruin
outline.gist: The elite used the language of patience for falsehood, appealing to ancestors and calling tawhid an invention; wars are started by speakers of falsehood.

outline.heading: Abu Jahl and Musaylimah's followers: tribal pride over truth
outline.gist: Abu Jahl admitted the Prophet was truthful but would not follow a prophet from Banu Hashim; Musaylimah's followers said a liar of Rabi'ah was better than a truthful man of Mudar.

38:2.en: Nay, but those who disbelieve are in false pride and schism

38:3.en: How many a generation We destroyed before them, and they cried out when it was no longer the time for escape

38:4.en: And they marvel that a warner from among themselves hath come unto them, and the disbelievers say: This is a wizard, a charlatan

38:8.en: Hath the reminder been unto him (alone) among us? Nay, but they are in doubt concerning My reminder; nay but they have not yet tasted My doom

38:13.ar: وَثَمُودُ وَقَوۡمُ لُوطࣲ وَأَصۡحَٰبُ لۡـَٔيۡكَةِۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ ٱلۡأَحۡزَابُ
38:13.en: And (the tribe of) Thamud, and the folk of Lot, and the dwellers in the wood: these were the factions

LTUkimnZteM.title: Arabic Tafsir of Surat Sad: Persisting in Falsehood and the Courage to Return, Verses 2-17
LTUkimnZteM.one_line: Why people persist in what they know is false, scholars who publicly retracted, the ego's resistance, and the promise that the confederates will be defeated.
LTUkimnZteM.summary: Continuing Surat Sad's theme of obeying Allah by returning to the truth, the sheikh argues that no Muslim is safe without it, because every person will at some point stand with falsehood. Quraysh defended falsehood by attacking the Prophet's person, mocking tawhid, dismissing it as unknown to their ancestors and urging patience with their gods. Abu Jahl, dying at Badr, still asked who had won the day, and it is shameful when people of truth are less committed than people of falsehood. He recounts two scholars he witnessed: Sh. Ayman Suwayd, who publicly retracted a tajweed position he had defended for twenty years, and Sh. Abdullah al-Asfar, who asked to be taught after being corrected on his first word, and links their later blessing to that humility. A good leader is not one who never errs but one who returns when wrong. The real obstacle is the commanding self, which knows only what benefits it now and fears losing status; tyrants fight tawhid because a believer in one God cannot be owned. Allah asks whether they hold the treasures of His mercy, gives the Prophet glad tidings that the confederates will be defeated, and lists nations destroyed for denial. Taktheeb, rejecting what one knows is right, breeds every vice; the Prophet is told to be patient and remember Dawud.

outline.heading: Rejecting an idea because the ancestors did not know it

outline.heading: Persisting in a wrong position for personal reasons
outline.gist: People keep a stance they know is wrong out of pride, hoping no one notices, or because bad advisers reassure them.

outline.heading: Sh. Ayman Suwayd retracted a position he held for twenty years
outline.gist: He had defended a tajweed view on iqlab and later told people openly that he had been wrong.

outline.heading: Sh. Abdullah al-Asfar asked to be taught
outline.gist: Corrected on his first word, the famous reciter said 'teach me', studied the ten readings and went on to lead a programme that reached a million memorisers.

outline.heading: Returning to the truth brings blessing
outline.gist: Humility and sincerity bring barakah in life, knowledge and family; Umar's standing came from stopping at the truth.

outline.heading: Abu Jahl's rivalry and the danger of persisting
outline.gist: He could not follow a man of Banu Hashim; persistence can confuse a person until he cannot tell truth from falsehood, as with Lut's people.

outline.heading: Recitation of verses 8-11
'Was the reminder sent down to him out of all of us?'
outline.gist: Their objections were his humanity and his person; Allah answers that an angel would remove the test of faith.

outline.heading: Falsehood worked for years; we too defend wrong choices
outline.gist: Their approach lasted over a decade; a good leader is the one who returns to the truth when he sees his choice was wrong.

outline.heading: You will err; the question is whether you return
outline.gist: If Allah is merciful your error will be in a minor matter; in a major one persistence leads to ruin.

outline.heading: 'They are in doubt about My reminder'
outline.gist: Some doubt always remains after weighing evidence; a reasonable person follows what is most likely and does not let leftover doubt steer him.

outline.heading: The commanding self only understands benefit now
outline.gist: Right and wrong mean nothing to the ego; tawhid demands selflessness, which the self resists.

outline.heading: Tyrants fight tawhid because a believer cannot be owned
outline.gist: One who fears only Allah cannot be pushed around; the commanding self is what blocks the return to truth.

outline.heading: Admitting you were wrong to someone you dislike is the hardest moment
outline.gist: Only a seeker of truth finds it easy, as Umar did on the minbar; 'they have not yet tasted My punishment'.

outline.heading: 'Do they hold the treasures of your Lord's mercy?'
outline.gist: Al-Aziz cannot be grasped and al-Wahhab gives without cause, so no one may question whom He chooses; if they own the heavens, let them climb the means.

outline.heading: 'A band of the confederates, defeated there'
outline.gist: 'Hunalika' signals glad tidings; revealed before the Prophet fled the plot on his life, it promised victory, most likely at Badr. Whoever persists in falsehood meets a painful end.

outline.heading: Recitation, and a story that begins mid-verse
outline.gist: Dawud's story starts within the verse to show it continues the same point.

outline.heading: Taktheeb is worse than disbelief
outline.gist: Kufr is absence of faith; taktheeb is rejecting faith while knowing it is more likely right.

outline.heading: The nations destroyed for persisting
outline.gist: Nuh, 'Ad, Pharaoh of the stakes, Thamud, Lut and the people of the thicket; not every nation in the Quran was destroyed.

outline.heading: Denial breeds every vice: Pharaoh and the nine signs
outline.gist: Every confrontation with truth deepened Pharaoh's persistence until Hell; a small stance can grow beyond return.

outline.heading: Awaiting a single blast
outline.gist: A threat that Allah did not carry out on Mecca, and many of them later believed.

outline.heading: 'Hasten our share before the Day of Reckoning'
outline.gist: Qitt was a written award, as in the poets al-Mutalammis and Tarafah; their mockery grew step by step until they challenged Allah.

outline.heading: Be patient, and remember Our servant Dawud
outline.gist: Dawud's story is a reminder to the Prophet himself to return to the truth; the Quran shows the failings of others so we avoid them.

outline.heading: The Prophet told to stop at the truth
outline.gist: A preview of a description of a prophet that the Companions heard for the first time in this surah.

UZXaWiX_WQA.title: Tackling Contemporary Issues: Marriage (Part 3)
UZXaWiX_WQA.one_line: Three points for keeping marriages: build on ihsan rather than rights, never tolerate abuse, and handle inevitable disputes wisely while protecting the children.
UZXaWiX_WQA.summary: In the last of three khutbahs on marriage, he says keeping marriages intact used to come naturally but is now failing. His first point is that Islamic marriage rests on ihsan: the obligations are few, a husband provides and protects and a wife stays loyal and cares for the children, so everything else is an act of love. When we treat extras as rights, any shortfall breeds resentment; when we see them as gifts, we feel grateful and give back. Men need respect and someone who stands by them in hard times, which he draws from the Prophet's lifelong love for Khadijah, who believed in him when others rejected him; women, he thinks, need to feel needed, loved and noticed. Second, abuse of any kind is never acceptable, though the term should be defined carefully, and the community must protect the abused and rehabilitate the abuser internally. Third, disputes are guaranteed even in the Prophet's household, so seek help from unbiased people who will tell you that you are wrong, not parents who inflame things. Divorce is sometimes right, as with Zayd and Zaynab, but children must never be weaponized. He closes by urging the community to invest its resources in helping people marry and stay married.

outline.gist: The obligations are few: the husband protects and provides food, clothing and a home; the wife stays loyal and cares for the children.

outline.heading: Obligation breeds no gratitude, extras do
outline.gist: Our parents' habits make the list seem longer; what is owed draws no thanks and its absence causes anger, while what is extra is received with appreciation, in both directions.

outline.heading: The reward of excellence is excellence
outline.gist: Extras answered with extras fill a marriage with the love and mercy Allah described; entitlement fills it with resentment, and what was extra to begin with should not upset you when missing.

outline.heading: What men need
outline.gist: It takes two to tango; men need to feel respected and to have someone stand by them when they are weak and come home burdened.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet married as he did
outline.gist: His later marriages were strategic: uniting tribes and the house of Abraham and giving eminent women autonomy at a hard time.

outline.heading: Aisha's jealousy of Khadijah
outline.gist: He loved Khadijah until he died; Aisha was jealous only of her, though she had died years earlier, and he sent portions of every gift to Khadijah's friends.

outline.heading: Khadijah's friends while an army waited
outline.gist: He halted an army and sat half an hour under a tree with three elderly women, reminiscing about Khadijah.

outline.heading: He knew her footsteps
outline.gist: Years after her death he sat up at footsteps that sounded like hers; told to remarry, he asked who could take her place.

outline.heading: She stood by me when others turned away
outline.gist: When Aisha said he had better, he answered that Khadijah believed in him and supported him when people rejected him; loyalty in hardship is what men remember.

outline.heading: What women need, and respect above love
outline.gist: From observation he thinks women want to feel needed, loved and attended to; for men respect matters even more than love, and weakening your husband makes no sense.

outline.heading: Even the best had marital quarrels
outline.gist: The Prophet found Ali sleeping on the masjid dust after a quarrel and sent him home; difficulties are part of life, but answer them with excellence and love.

outline.heading: Interlude
Point two: abuse is never acceptable
outline.gist: Physical, verbal, financial or social abuse is never allowed, but the term, especially emotional abuse, must be defined carefully; it happens in both directions and the abused must be protected.

outline.heading: The Prophet never struck anyone
outline.gist: Good people with bad tempers still abuse, and society must protect the other party; nothing in Islam permits abuse, and the Prophet never raised his hand except in combat.

outline.heading: Deal with abuse within the community
outline.gist: Outsiders handling our cases do not share our values; families and friends must not look away, the abused must be protected and the abuser educated and treated.

outline.heading: Point three: disputes are guaranteed
outline.gist: Every married couple will fight; being patient with and caring for a spouse is worship for both, and disputes are the salt of marriage.

outline.heading: Parents usually make it worse
outline.gist: Seek help when needed, but parents and relatives come in biased and outraged on their child's behalf and ruin homes.

outline.heading: Ask those who will tell you you're wrong
outline.gist: Choose helpers who will say you are wrong, not ones who egg you on; even the Prophet withdrew from his wives to an upper room, so disputes reach every home.

outline.heading: When divorce is needed: Zayd and Zaynab
outline.gist: Divorce is right when abuse cannot be fixed or spouses keep harming each other; two of the best companions could not make it work, but seek proper counselling first.

outline.heading: Do not weaponize your children
outline.gist: Children did nothing to deserve the conflict and cannot understand it; argue behind a closed door, because their only stability is the two of you and its loss surfaces years later.

outline.heading: Protecting them is what masculinity means
outline.gist: Whether or not you love your spouse, you must protect and provide for your children; masculinity in Islam is responsibility, not control, and divorce becomes the answer when the children are being harmed.

outline.heading: Interlude
Invest in the family
outline.gist: These are observed patterns, not a full guide; the community must spend its time, wealth and resources helping people marry, stay married and resolve disputes, or the masjid will be empty in a generation.

outline.heading: Outro

M9CeoCd_bLw.title: Arabic Tafsir of Surat as-Saffat: Surrendering to the Unseen, the Closing Verses 149-182
M9CeoCd_bLw.one_line: Knowledge that exists versus knowledge that is withheld: why believers surrender to the unseen, answer with tasbih, and know their appointed station.
M9CeoCd_bLw.summary: Closing Surat as-Saffat, the sheikh names its axis: obedience and surrender to Allah in matters of the unseen whose wisdom we cannot reach. Citing al-Tahawi, he distinguishes knowledge that exists in creation, which we must pursue, from knowledge that is withheld, whose pursuit leads to disbelief. Demanding to grasp Allah's essence before believing is a logical fallacy, since a god you could comprehend would not be God. He applies this to obsessive interest in jinn, possession and magic, which breeds superstition, and to people who speak confidently on what they do not know, insisting it is fine not to know and that one should not invent explanations, as with the hadith of the fly. The Quran's challenge to those who called the angels daughters of Allah, 'bring your book', exposes claims without evidence that also degraded women. The response to what we cannot understand is tasbih, as Yunus was saved by glorifying Allah. The believers' words 'each of us has a known station' teach us to know our purpose and our rows in prayer, while leaving the angels' rows to Allah, unlike those who argued over the number nineteen. The final verses, likely revealed before the Hijrah, assure the Prophet that messengers will be victorious even when the wisdom of leaving Mecca was hidden.

outline.heading: The axis: surrender in matters of the unseen; al-Tahawi's two kinds of knowledge
outline.gist: Rejecting knowledge that exists and claiming knowledge that is withheld are both disbelief; modern people expect science to answer everything.

outline.heading: Allah's essence cannot be grasped
outline.gist: The wisdom of a command may be found later, but the essence of Allah cannot; we can know Him through love, nearness and obedience. A mind built for beginnings and ends cannot grasp the eternal.

outline.heading: Refusing to believe until you understand Allah is a fallacy
outline.gist: A god whose essence you could comprehend would not be God; as-Saffat opens with angels, jinn, resurrection and the tree of Zaqqum, all unseen.

outline.heading: Prophets were made to do what they did not understand
outline.gist: Why Yunus was swallowed, why his people were spared and Lut's were not: we do not know.

outline.heading: Pursue existing knowledge, invest in knowing Allah
outline.gist: Fiqh, belief, seerah and applied sciences are to be pursued; knowledge of Allah's names, attributes and acts raises you, while chasing the inaccessible is beating your head on a wall.

outline.heading: Jinn, possession and magic: withheld knowledge breeds superstition
outline.gist: The Quran and Sunnah tell us very little about jinn and nothing about entering bodies; claims without evidence lead to harm and superstition.

outline.gist: The Quran demands witness or evidence; ifk is a lie with no truth in it at all, as in the slander of Aishah.

outline.heading: False claims about Allah's offspring degraded women
outline.gist: Choosing daughters for Allah and sons for themselves produced a baseless hierarchy that buried girls; 'bring your book if you are truthful'.

outline.heading: Speaking without knowledge harms people
outline.gist: Everyone acts as a doctor with folk remedies; it is normal and acceptable not to know most things.

outline.heading: Do not invent explanations: the hadith of the fly
outline.gist: He accepts the hadith without knowing its wisdom rather than fabricating research to defend it.

outline.heading: Surrender to the unseen comes after faith is built
outline.gist: As-Saffat is not meant to build faith but to follow it; there are calamities no scholar can explain, and this generation is used to having an answer for everything.

outline.heading: Kinship invented between Allah and the jinn
outline.gist: They claimed the angels' mothers were jinn; the jinn know they too will be brought to judgment.

outline.heading: Tasbih is the answer to what we cannot understand
outline.gist: Yunus did not object but glorified Allah and was saved; 'subhanallah' is acceptance of hidden wisdom, not mere wonder.

outline.heading: Recitation with tajweed notes
outline.gist: A necessary madd before a shaddah is six counts in Hafs from Asim by the Shatibiyyah route.

outline.heading: You cannot tempt anyone except one headed for the Fire
outline.gist: The chosen sincere servants are exempt; he explains why the ya of 'sali' is dropped and why stopping there is a bad pause.

outline.heading: 'Each of us has a known station'
outline.gist: He prefers that these are the believers' words: Allah has fixed each person's place in this world and the next.

outline.heading: Your known station is your purpose
outline.gist: Where you came from, why you are here, what is asked of you and where you are going; animals live by herd instinct, but humans must ask.

outline.heading: Our rows are known; the angels' rows are not
outline.gist: We know our rows in prayer and our tasbih; how the angels stand in rows is withheld knowledge we entrust to Allah.

outline.heading: Chasing withheld details: the number of the cave's companions and the nineteen
outline.gist: Counting the companions of the cave or mocking the nineteen guardians of Hell misses the point; the believer only grows in faith.

outline.heading: The sincere servants accept Allah's command seen or unseen
outline.gist: Mukhlas is one Allah has purified for Himself because he obeys whether he understands or not; the Quran opens with belief in the unseen.

outline.heading: Recitation of the final verses
Messengers will be victorious: revealed before the Hijrah
outline.gist: Unlike Yunus, the Prophet left with permission but as a fugitive; the promise holds even when victory is not visible, as for Muslims scattered in Abyssinia and fleeing Mecca.

outline.heading: Turn away from them for a while and watch
outline.gist: Do your work and leave the timing to Allah; Allah chose not to destroy the people of Mecca while the Prophet was among them.

outline.heading: Closing with tasbih and praise
outline.gist: The Lord of might is beyond reach; when wisdom is hidden, glorify Him, then praise Him.

4:34.en: Men are in charge of women, because Allah hath made the one of them to excel the other, and because they spend of their property (for the support of women). So good women are the obedient, guarding in secret that which Allah hath guarded. As for those from whom ye fear rebellion, admonish them and banish them to beds apart, and scourge them. Then if they obey you, seek not a way against them. Lo! Allah is ever High, Exalted, Great

01BnvGcttl8.title: Tackling Contemporary Issues: Marriage (Part 2)
01BnvGcttl8.one_line: Find a spouse through your social network, agree on roles before marrying, know the Islamic default, and understand that male responsibility brings leadership.
01BnvGcttl8.summary: Opening with the verse that men are caretakers of women, he continues his marriage series with points on initiating and structuring a marriage. Spouses have always been found through social networks, so parents and siblings should be involved, though the choice stays with the individual; he has seen no good outcomes from apps. Next, the verse allowing spouses to agree on anything beyond the pillars of nikah means couples must use the courtship period to discuss roles and expectations rather than romance. Couples today come from very different backgrounds, so mismatched expectations are like driving into a wall. He gives his own arrangement as one valid option and tells Umar's story from Musnad Ahmad: Makkan men controlled their wives while Madinan women argued back, the Prophet's wives included, and the Quran did not condemn either norm. In the second khutbah he sets out the Islamic default either spouse can always return to: the husband provides financially and the wife is responsible for caregiving, by herself or someone she arranges. He adds that with responsibility comes leadership, meaning protection not dictatorship, and warns against erasing masculinity and femininity because going against nature rarely works.

outline.heading: Opening
Men as caretakers of women
outline.gist: An-Nisa verse: men are caretakers because of what Allah has favoured them with and what they spend; the base text for the khutbah.

outline.heading: Point one: find a spouse through your social network
outline.gist: Second of three marriage khutbahs; the idea of 'the one' among eight billion is a delusion; spouses have always come through family and friends, such as a relative of a friend's wife.

outline.heading: Involve your parents, but the choice is yours
outline.gist: He has yet to see apps work out well; parents and siblings know you best and must weigh in, while choosing remains your right; parents withdrawing from this role is unwise for a lifelong bond.

outline.heading: Point two: whatever spouses agree is valid
outline.gist: An-Nisa verse: no blame for what spouses agree beyond the pillars of nikah (guardian, witnesses, dowry, consent).

outline.heading: Roles before romance
outline.gist: Couples waste the courtship on romance; entering marriage with mismatched roles and expectations is driving at 200 km/h into a brick wall.

outline.heading: Different backgrounds, and his own arrangement
outline.gist: His grandfather never needed the conversation, but today's mixed ummah does; he asked for a homemaker because of his schedule, and a neurosurgeon saying no would have been equally right.

outline.heading: Ibn Abbas asks Umar about the two wives
outline.gist: On a journey Ibn Abbas carries Umar's wudu water and asks who the two wives in the verse were, a question Umar dislikes because one was his daughter.

outline.heading: Makkah and Madinah: Umar's wife argues back
outline.gist: Umar names Aisha and Hafsa; Makkan men had full authority over wives while Madinan women did not, and when his wife argued back she pointed to the Prophet's wives doing the same.

outline.heading: Umar warns Hafsa
outline.gist: Shaken, Umar goes to Hafsa, asks whether the Prophet's wives argue with him, and warns her not to imitate Aisha.

outline.heading: More than one way to run a family
outline.gist: Hafsa did it anyway and the Quran did not condemn either norm; Islam allows different arrangements, so agree on the important matters before children are involved.

outline.heading: Ask your father what to look for
outline.gist: Young men who do not know what they want should ask their fathers; what was never discussed up front cannot be changed later.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Islamic default
outline.gist: Either spouse can always return to the default: the husband provides financially, the wife is responsible for the physical caregiving of the children and the integrity of the home.

outline.heading: Either spouse may revert to it
outline.gist: A working wife can ask him to become sole provider; he can ask her to take charge of caregiving, which does not stop her working, and her earnings then remain hers alone.

outline.heading: Caregivers and dual-professional couples
outline.gist: If she will not do the caregiving herself she arranges someone; two physicians or lawyers will need a third person, which is not haram, but how it is funded must be agreed.

outline.heading: With responsibility comes leadership: the protector
outline.gist: The man is accountable before Allah and is always the protector, not a dictator; like the Titanic, his life comes after his wife's and children's.

outline.heading: A pilot with a co-pilot
outline.gist: Two people cannot steer at once; the wife may hold the wheel on a matter, but he remains responsible for the outcome.

outline.heading: Obedience within protection
outline.gist: Obedience to the husband applies when he is protecting the family's safety; sisters should not want a man who does not feel he is its leader and protector.

outline.heading: Preserve masculinity and femininity
outline.gist: A strong, brave, confident husband and a wife who is cared for and not overburdened; this delicate balance is no place for experiments.

outline.heading: Going against nature
outline.gist: Even outside religion, discarding the value of masculine and feminine traits rarely works; recap of the three points, with the abuse of these roles next week.

outline.heading: Outro
